title: Companies Are Spending Too Much on Stock Buybacks
text:

https://www.barrons.com/articles/companies-are-spending-too-much-on-stock-buybacks-51546275170 Companies Are Spending Too Much on Stock Buybacks By Updated Dec. 31, 2018 3:10 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Benjamin Child Text size
Last year’s tax overhaul reduced the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21%, leaving companies with a lot more after-tax profits to spend as they pleased.
Companies could have used the additional cash to build factories, buy equipment, and invest in new technologies — costs that are known as capital expenditures, or capex for short. Looking back, however, much of the tax savings were used by companies to buy back their own stocks — usually at expensive prices — only to see the value evaporate in the year-end market turmoil. Markets continued to fall after Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin tried to instill calm following a bruising week. WSJ’s Ken Brown explains why investors are unloading stocks. Photo: AP
Apple (AAPL), for example, spent about $62.9 billion on buybacks in the first nine months of 2018, but those shares were worth only $53.8 billion as of Dec. 26 , according to the Wall Street Journal. That’s a $9.1 billion — or 14.5% loss — in investment return.
Apple wasn’t alone. In the first nine months of 2018, S&P 500 companies bought back $583.4 billion worth of their own shares, up 52.6% from the same period in 2017, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices . The S&P 500 has dropped 6.4% since the start of the year.
To be sure, companies did spend on capital improvements. Fixed investments increased 11.5% in the first quarter of 2018, and 8.5% in the second quarter compared with same periods in 2017. The boost, however, faded in the third quarter : Capital spending rose just 0.8% from July through September, according to data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis .
Too many uncertainties in the macro environment — including higher tariffs, slowing global demand, and rising interest rates — might have deterred companies from further investment and expansion. This, however, might not a logical choice over the long run, according some strategists.
Companies usually use “cost of equity capital” — the required rate of return that stockholders demand to compensate for the market risk — as a benchmark to assess whether a new capital investment is worth it. Investment opportunities that don’t top that bar are usually considered unfeasible, so the money goes to buybacks and dividends as a way to return excess cash to shareholders.
But there is a good chance that the rate of return companies are using is too high, claims DataTrek’s Nicholas Colas . The average chief financial officer would likely set the cost of equity capital at around 10%, a high bar to reach, Colas writes. The actual cost is probably close to 5%, which would allow CFO’s to be more aggressive in their capex investment decisions. And that miscalculation comes with a cost. “Rather than invest in marginal projects, they try to buttress their stock’s valuation with buybacks,” writes Colas, “That’s a sensible approach in a micro sense, but markets see a macro environment where companies forsake long-term growth for short-term stock returns.”
Ned Davis , senior investment strategist at Ned Davis Research , holds the same opinion. He noted that since 1950, cost to buy back stocks — measured by the growth of all equity market value — were on average 25% higher than the cost to replace existing assets on the book. In other words, “it costs less to purchase new investment assets than it does to buy back stocks,” Davis writes.
Even record-breaking buybacks couldn’t save the market this year. The S&P 500 is now down 14% from peak and almost entered a bear market on the Christmas Eve. With such volatility in the market, betting too much on one’s own stock might not be such a good idea in terms of capital allocation.
